summary: Mexico's exports hit a record $389.7 billion, helping the economy grow 1.5% in the second quarter, above forecasts. The US trade office is nearing a decision on Mexico's manufacturing capacity under a Section 301 investigation ahead of August talks, though Fitch says the US effective tariff rate on Mexican goods has eased to 3.7%. Separately, an arbitration panel closed part of Vulcan Materials' dispute with Mexico, while Pemex admitted financial reporting errors spanning three presidential terms, complicating its access to financing.

lead.h1: US trade office nears decision on Mexico's manufacturing capacity as exports hit a record
lead.context: A ruling under a Section 301 investigation could bring new tariffs as August talks with Washington approach, even as Mexico's exports reached $389.7 billion, a record.
lead.background: Section 301 is a US trade law tool that lets Washington investigate practices it considers unfair and impose tariffs outside the normal dispute process, separate from the annual US-Mexico-Canada trade agreement review.
lead.view: A pending 301 ruling on Mexico's manufacturing capacity could add tariffs on top of existing measures even as exports set a record. The first half's $389.7 billion is close to sixty percent of all of 2025's $665 billion in goods exports, so volume is not what Washington is targeting, the composition and origin of that capacity is. Exporters gain little from record shipments if the review focuses on how components enter Mexican supply chains rather than how much crosses the border.
lead.prediction: New tariffs or a negotiated carve-out are more likely than inaction once the August talks conclude. That expectation would be wrong if US trade office delays the ruling past the talks or folds the issue into the broader annual review of the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement instead of acting on its own.

coverage.summary: A ruling under a Section 301 investigation could bring new tariffs as August talks with Washington approach, even as Mexico's exports reached $389.7 billion, a record.

items.headline: Mexico's economy grows 1.5% in second quarter, beating forecasts
items.context: Growth was driven by record exports and consumption tied to the World Cup, offering an upside surprise amid ongoing trade tensions with the United States.
items.background: Mexico's statistics agency reports quarterly economic growth against the prior three-month period, a different measure from the annual figure. Full-year 2025 growth was only about 0.6%, so a single strong quarter needs that pace as context.
items.view: The 1.5% quarter-on-quarter gain beat forecasts of 1.4%, but exports and World Cup-related spending are one-off drivers rather than proof of a durable shift in the growth rate. Fixed investment fell from 23.8% to 22.4% of gross domestic product in 2025, the number that would need to reverse before a strong export quarter turns into lasting capacity. A record export quarter can coexist with the same weak link between trade and household income that produced 2025's 0.6% growth.
items.prediction: The most likely path is a slowdown in the third quarter once World Cup consumption fades, unless investment data show new capacity being built rather than existing plants running harder. That would be contradicted by a rise in the investment share of gross domestic product alongside continued export strength.

items.headline: Arbitration panel closes part of Vulcan Materials' dispute with the Mexican government
items.context: The ruling ends part of a long-running conflict over the company's limestone quarry in Quintana Roo, a case that strained relations during the previous administration.
items.background: Vulcan Materials' dispute over its limestone quarry in Quintana Roo began under the López Obrador administration, when the government pursued decrees and a possible land purchase, prompting the company to pursue litigation and an international arbitration claim.
items.view: The ruling closes one arbitration claim, not the underlying dispute over the quarry's status. Vulcan gains a narrow legal win while broader questions over land use and future decrees remain open. Arbitration's ability to resolve discrete claims incrementally, rather than the whole case at once, is what lets the company bank partial certainty without ending the conflict.
items.prediction: Vulcan and the Mexican government are more likely to keep negotiating remaining claims than to reach a full settlement soon. That would be wrong if the two sides announce a comprehensive resolution or the company divests the Quintana Roo operation.

items.headline: Fitch says the US effective tariff rate on Mexican goods eases to 3.7%
items.context: The rating agency's estimate reflects changes in US trade policy and trade flows, easing concern over the tariff burden on Mexican exports even as broader negotiations continue.
items.background: The United States taxes Mexican exports through overlapping tariff regimes, including duties tied to Section 301 authority and country-specific rates that depend on whether goods meet the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement's regional-content rules.
items.view: An effective tariff rate of 3.7% looks manageable next to blanket duties elsewhere, but the figure blends US-Mexico-Canada trade agreement-compliant goods entering tariff-free with non-compliant goods facing a 10% rate or higher sectoral tariffs, so it masks which exporters are actually exposed. The rate could shift again once the pending Section 301 ruling on manufacturing capacity is decided, since that case sits outside the calculation Fitch used.
items.prediction: The effective tariff rate is likely to stay near this level only until the Section 301 ruling is issued, at which point it could move in either direction depending on the decision. That view would be wrong if the rate changes without any new US tariff action, which would mean trade-flow shifts rather than policy are driving it.

items.headline: Pemex acknowledges financial reporting errors spanning three presidential terms
items.context: The state oil company's admission of accounting problems dating back years could complicate its access to financing at a time when investors are already wary of its debt load.
items.background: Pemex files a 6-K report with the US Securities and Exchange Commission because it carries dollar-denominated bonds held by US investors, obligating disclosure of material weaknesses in its financial controls.
items.view: The admission matters because it confirms internal control failures persisted through five different directors and three presidential terms rather than being isolated to one administration. Pemex is not financially separate from the federal government, so weaker credibility with bondholders raises the cost of the sovereign-backed refinancing that keeps the company afloat, at a time when that support already competes with spending on grids and water for new factories.
items.prediction: Pemex is likely to face higher borrowing costs or tighter covenant terms on its next bond issuance or refinancing round. That would be contradicted if global investors price new Pemex debt at spreads similar to prior issuances despite the disclosed control weaknesses.
